claim: A CloudTrail event record shows who made the request (userIdentity), what was requested (eventSource and eventName), when it was completed (eventTime) and where it came from (sourceIPAddress).
q: Which fields of a CloudTrail record show who, what, when and from where?
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-record-contents
Information about the IAM identity that made a request.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-record-contents
The service that the request was made to.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-record-contents
The requested action, which is one of the actions in the API for that service.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-record-contents
The date and time the request was completed, in coordinated universal time (UTC).
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-record-contents
The IP address that the request was made from.

claim: CloudTrail logs attempts to sign in to the AWS Management Console, the AWS Discussion Forums and the AWS Support Center; all IAM user, root user and federated user sign-in events generate records in CloudTrail log files.
q: Does CloudTrail record failed or successful console sign-ins?
v: sign in to the AWS Management Console
All IAM user and root user sign-in events
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-event-reference-aws-console-sign-in-events

CloudTrail logs attempts to sign in to the AWS Management Console, the AWS Discussion Forums, and the AWS Support Center. All IAM user and root user sign-in events, as well as all federated user sign-in events, generate records in CloudTrail log files.

claim: CloudTrail also logs non-API AWS service events, which are created by AWS services but are not directly triggered by a request to a public AWS API; for these events the eventType field is AwsServiceEvent.
q: Does CloudTrail log events that are not API calls?
v: not directly triggered by a request
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-non-api-events

[AWS service events](non-api-aws-service-events.md) – CloudTrail supports logging non-API service events. These events are created by AWS services but are not directly triggered by a request to a public AWS API. For these events, the `eventType` field is `AwsServiceEvent`.

claim: You can deliver one copy of your ongoing management events to your S3 bucket at no charge from CloudTrail by creating a trail, but Amazon S3 storage charges apply.
q: What do you pay for when you create a trail for management events?
v: one copy of your ongoing management events
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide
You can deliver one copy of your ongoing management events to your S3 bucket at no charge from CloudTrail by creating a trail, however, there are Amazon S3 storage charges.

claim: If a trail is misconfigured, for example the S3 bucket is unreachable, CloudTrail attempts to redeliver the log files to the bucket for 30 days, and these attempts are subject to standard CloudTrail charges; deleting the trail avoids the charges.
q: What happens if the S3 bucket of a trail is unreachable?
v: redeliver the log files to your S3 bucket
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/how-cloudtrail-works

If you misconfigure your trail (for example, the S3 bucket is unreachable), CloudTrail will attempt to redeliver the log files to your S3 bucket for 30 days, and these attempted-to-deliver events will be subject to standard CloudTrail charges. To avoid charges on a misconfigured trail, you need to delete the trail.

claim: AWS CloudTrail Lake lets you run SQL-based queries on your events, which are aggregated into event data stores that are immutable collections of events.
q: Which CloudTrail option lets you run SQL queries over events?
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake
AWS CloudTrail Lake lets you run SQL-based queries on your events.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake

Events are aggregated into event data stores, which are immutable collections of events based on criteria that you select by applying [advanced event selectors](cloudtrail-lake-concepts.md#adv-event-selectors).

claim: You can keep event data in a CloudTrail Lake event data store for up to 3,653 days (about 10 years) with the One-year extendable retention pricing option, or up to 2,557 days (about 7 years) with the Seven-year retention pricing option.
q: How long can CloudTrail Lake keep event data?
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide

You can keep the event data in an event data store for up to 3,653 days (about 10 years) if you choose the **One-year extendable retention pricing** option, or up to 2,557 days (about 7 years) if you choose the **Seven-year retention pricing** option.

claim: CloudTrail Lake event data stores and queries incur charges; the pricing option you choose determines the cost for ingesting and storing events and the default and maximum retention period, and queries are charged by the amount of data scanned.
q: What do you pay for in CloudTrail Lake?
v: pay based upon the amount of data scanned
The pricing option determines the cost
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide

CloudTrail Lake event data stores and queries incur charges. When you create an event data store, you choose the [pricing option](cloudtrail-lake-manage-costs.md#cloudtrail-lake-manage-costs-pricing-option) you want to use for the event data store. The pricing option determines the cost for ingesting and storing events, and the default and maximum retention period for the event data store. When you run queries in Lake, you pay based upon the amount of data scanned.

claim: AWS CloudTrail Lake will no longer be open to new customers starting on May 31, 2026, existing customers can continue to use it as normal, and CloudTrail trails, Insights and aggregated events are not affected.
q: Can a new customer start using CloudTrail Lake?
v: no longer be open to new customers
Trails, Insights and Aggregated Events are not affected
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake-service-availability-change
AWS CloudTrail Lake will no longer be open to new customers starting on May 31, 2026.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake-service-availability-change
Existing customers can continue to use the service as normal.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake-service-availability-change
Only AWS CloudTrail Lake is no longer open to new customers. Your AWS CloudTrail Trails, Insights and Aggregated Events are not affected.

claim: AWS recommends that CloudTrail Lake customers migrate their CloudTrail Lake log data to Amazon CloudWatch, and says CloudTrail continues to be available while CloudTrail Lake only receives critical bug fixes and security updates.
q: What does AWS recommend for CloudTrail Lake customers?
v: migrate your AWS CloudTrail Lake logs data
only receive critical bug fixes and security updates
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake-service-availability-change
We recommend that you migrate your AWS CloudTrail Lake logs data to Amazon CloudWatch.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-lake-service-availability-change
AWS CloudTrail continues to be available for existing customers, but CloudTrail Lake will only receive critical bug fixes and security updates.

claim: The CloudTrail security best practices recommend creating a multi-Region trail to obtain a complete record of events taken by an IAM identity or service in your account, and creating one trail for management events in all Regions plus additional trails for specific event types.
q: What do the CloudTrail best practices recommend for a complete record of activity?
v: additional trails that log specific event types
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
To obtain a complete record of events taken by an IAM identity, or service in your AWS account, create a multi-Region trail.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security

To help manage your CloudTrail data, consider creating one trail that logs management events in all AWS Regions, and then creating additional trails that log specific event types for resources, such as Amazon S3 bucket activity or AWS Lambda functions.

claim: The CloudTrail security best practices recommend logging to a dedicated and centralized Amazon S3 bucket to enforce strict security controls, access and segregation of duties, and creating a separate AWS account as a log archive account.
q: Where should CloudTrail logs for many accounts be stored according to best practice?
v: a dedicated and centralized Amazon S3 bucket
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
By logging to a dedicated and centralized Amazon S3 bucket, you can enforce strict security controls, access, and segregation of duties.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
Create a separate AWS account as a log archive account.

claim: The CloudTrail security best practices recommend least privilege access to the S3 buckets that store log files, and MFA delete so that attempts to change the versioning state of the bucket or delete an object version need additional authentication.
q: How can you protect CloudTrail log files in S3 from being deleted?
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
In order to help ensure that integrity, you should adhere to the principle of least privilege when creating or modifying access to any Amazon S3 bucket used for storing CloudTrail log files.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
When you configure multi-factor authentication (MFA), attempts to change the versioning state of bucket, or delete an object version in a bucket, require additional authentication.

claim: As a security best practice, AWS recommends adding an aws:SourceArn condition key to the S3 bucket policy for CloudTrail logs, and adding an aws:SourceArn (or optionally aws:SourceAccount) condition key to the SNS topic policy statement.
q: Which condition key does AWS recommend on the CloudTrail bucket policy and SNS topic policy?
v: condition key to the bucket policy
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
As a security best practice, be sure to manually add a `aws:SourceArn` condition key to the bucket policy.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
As a security best practice, we recommend adding an `aws:SourceArn` (or optionally `aws:SourceAccount`) condition key to the Amazon SNS topic policy statement.

claim: The CloudTrail security best practices recommend integrating with CloudWatch Logs, which allows you to monitor and receive alerts for specific events captured by CloudTrail, such as failed AWS Management Console sign-in events.
q: How can you get alerts for specific events that CloudTrail captures?
v: monitor and receive alerts for specific events
failed AWS Management Console sign-in events
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security
CloudWatch Logs allows you to monitor and receive alerts for specific events captured by CloudTrail.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/best-practices-security

For example, you can monitor key security and network-related management events, such as [failed AWS Management Console sign-in events](cloudwatch-alarms-for-cloudtrail.md#cloudwatch-alarms-for-cloudtrail-signin).

claim: You can define an interface VPC endpoint for CloudTrail to connect your VPC to CloudTrail without an internet gateway, NAT instance or VPN connection; interface VPC endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink.
q: How can instances in a VPC reach the CloudTrail API without using the internet?
ev: docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-and-interface-VPC
The endpoint provides reliable, scalable connectivity to CloudTrail without requiring an internet gateway, network address translation (NAT) instance, or VPN connection.
docs/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-and-interface-VPC
Interface VPC endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink, an AWS technology that enables private communication between AWS services using an elastic network interface with private IP addresses.

claim: You can define an interface VPC endpoint for CloudWatch to connect your VPC to CloudWatch without an internet gateway, NAT instance or VPN connection; interface VPC endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink.
q: How can instances in a VPC reach CloudWatch without using the internet?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-and-interface-VPC

The endpoint provides reliable, scalable connectivity to CloudWatch and supported CloudWatch services without requiring an internet gateway, network address translation (NAT) instance, or VPN connection.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-and-interface-VPC
Interface VPC endpoints are powered by AWS PrivateLink, an AWS technology that enables private communication between AWS services using an elastic network interface with private IP addresses.

claim: With an interface VPC endpoint for CloudWatch Logs you can send logs to CloudWatch Logs from your VPC without sending them through the internet.
q: How can a private VPC send logs to CloudWatch Logs without internet access?
v: private connection between your VPC and CloudWatch Logs
without sending them through the internet
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/cloudwatch-logs-and-interface-VPC

If you use Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) to host your AWS resources, you can establish a private connection between your VPC and CloudWatch Logs. You can use this connection to send logs to CloudWatch Logs without sending them through the internet.

claim: CloudWatch is integrated with CloudTrail: CloudTrail captures API calls made by or on behalf of your account, including calls from the CloudWatch console and code calls to CloudWatch API operations, so you can see the request, the IP address and when it was made.
q: Are CloudWatch API calls recorded in CloudTrail?
v: on behalf of your AWS account
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/logging_cw_api_calls
CloudTrail captures API calls made by or on behalf of your AWS account. The captured calls include calls from the CloudWatch console and code calls to CloudWatch API operations.

claim: CloudTrail can capture CloudWatch data plane operations on metrics such as GetMetricData, PutMetricData, GetMetricStatistics and ListMetrics as data events, but by default CloudTrail does not log data events and additional charges apply.
q: Does CloudTrail log PutMetricData and GetMetricData calls by default?
v: By default, CloudTrail doesn't log data events
Additional charges apply for data events
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/logging_cw_api_calls
CloudTrail can capture API activities related to the CloudWatch data plane operations on metrics GetMetricData, GetMetricWidgetImage, PutMetricData, GetMetricStatistics, and ListMetrics APIs.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/logging_cw_api_calls
By default, CloudTrail doesn't log data events. The CloudTrail **Event history** doesn't record data events.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/logging_cw_api_calls
Additional charges apply for data events.
